source: Erol, Hendler, Nau (1994) HTN Planning: Complexity and Expressivity (AAAI-94)
finding: First formal account of what an HTN planner is. Input: an initial task network, operators for primitive tasks, and methods (task, task network) for compound tasks. Planning repeatedly reduces a non-primitive task by a matching method until only primitive tasks remain, then finds a ground ordering that meets all constraints.
numbers: Three task types: goal tasks, primitive tasks, compound tasks. A method is a pair m=(t,d).
quote: One way of achieving the task is to achieve the task network d
limits: Theory paper, no empirical test. Critics (ordering, resource checks) are left out of the worst-case analysis.
agent_relevance: This is the exact shape of our O3: a method library maps a task to subtasks with constraints; the program expands until only directly doable steps remain.

source: Erol, Hendler, Nau (1994) HTN Planning: Complexity and Expressivity (AAAI-94)
finding: Whether a plan exists depends mostly on restrictions on non-primitive tasks. With no restrictions and no total order, HTN planning is undecidable even without variables. Either a total order or a restriction on non-primitive tasks alone restores decidability.
numbers: No restrictions, not totally ordered: undecidable. No restrictions, totally ordered, no variables: in EXPTIME, PSPACE-hard; with variables: EXPSPACE-hard, in DEXPTIME. 'Regular' (at most one non-primitive task, last): PSPACE-complete (no variables) or EXPSPACE-complete (variables). No non-primitive tasks: NP-complete, or polynomial if totally ordered and no variables.
limits: Worst-case results. They say nothing about typical practice where hand-made methods guide search.
agent_relevance: A free recursive decomposer is unbounded in the worst case. O3 needs hard limits (depth, node budget) and a fixed method library, as the theory predicts.

source: Erol, Hendler, Nau (1994) HTN Planning: Complexity and Expressivity (AAAI-94)
finding: HTN is strictly more expressive than STRIPS-style operators. Any STRIPS domain converts to an HTN domain in low-order polynomial time, but some HTN domains cannot be written as any finite set of STRIPS operators. This contradicts the view that HTN is just an efficiency hack.
numbers: Theorem 7: there exist HTN domains not representable by any finite set of STRIPS operators. Restricting methods to be regular gives STRIPS-equivalent power (like regular grammars).
quote: HTN's are more expressive than STRIPS-style operators.
limits: The extra power comes with undecidability in the unrestricted case.
agent_relevance: A method library can state procedures (compound tasks such as a round trip) that a goal-only scheme cannot. Keep tasks, not only goals, as O3 outputs.

source: Erol, Hendler, Nau (1996) Complexity results for HTN planning (Ann. Math. AI 18)
finding: Journal version gives the full proofs. Undecidability holds even when the planning domain is fixed in advance. Regular problems with variables stay EXPSPACE-complete, so even the STRIPS-equivalent subset is hard.
numbers: Theorem 4: totally ordered, variables allowed: EXPSPACE-hard, in DOUBLE-EXPTIME. Theorem 5: regular: EXPSPACE-complete, still so when totally ordered. Table I footnote: undecidable even with a fixed domain.
limits: Still worst-case. Proofs use encodings of grammar intersection and of STRIPS operator sets.
agent_relevance: Decomposition cost can blow up; a bound on expansion is a safety need, not a convenience.

source: Erol, Hendler, Nau (1996) Complexity results for HTN planning (Ann. Math. AI 18)
finding: Expressivity is compared formally. Theorem 9: no computable transformation from HTN planning problems to STRIPS-style problems exists in general. The 1994 claim of extra power is therefore proved, not argued.
numbers: Theorem 9 (non-existence of a computable translation). Languages are compared by which solution sets they can express.
limits: Only for unrestricted HTN; restricted classes (TIHTN, regular) can be translated.
agent_relevance: Do not expect a goal-only planner to replace a method library when the procedure itself is what matters.

source: Nau, Cao, Lotem, Munoz-Avila (1999) SHOP: Simple Hierarchical Ordered Planner (IJCAI-99)
finding: SHOP plans tasks in the order they will be executed, so it always knows the full current state. That keeps the algorithm simple, allows rich preconditions (numeric calculation, axioms), and lets domain knowledge prune most of the search.
numbers: Claim: several orders of magnitude faster than Blackbox and several times faster than TLplan, though SHOP is in Lisp and the others in C.
limits: Needs hand-written methods per domain. Tests were blocks world and logistics on 1990s hardware (167-MHz Sun).
agent_relevance: Ordered decomposition (expand the first open step with the current state known) fits a code-checked state in our schema best.

source: Nau, Cao, Lotem, Munoz-Avila (1999) SHOP: Simple Hierarchical Ordered Planner (IJCAI-99)
finding: Head-to-head logistics results. Blackbox needs tens to thousands of seconds; SHOP and TLplan need seconds or less, and SHOP matches or beats TLplan on plan length.
limits: SHOP used domain-tailored methods against a domain-independent Blackbox. The gain comes from the knowledge author, not the algorithm alone. Few problems.
agent_relevance: Quantifies what a good method library buys: about three orders of magnitude on the same problems. The value is in library quality.

source: Nau, Cao, Lotem, Munoz-Avila (1999) SHOP: Simple Hierarchical Ordered Planner (IJCAI-99)
finding: The logistics methods are a short ordered list of else-if rules (for example: if a plane holds packages, fly it to a destination of one; else if packages need pick-up, drive a truck to one; else deliver from a truck). A few lines of advice remove almost all backtracking.
numbers: 5-rule logistics method; blocks-world algorithm of Gupta and Nau encoded as methods; in the travel example SHOP found all plans in under 0.01 s.
limits: Rules are specific to the domain and problem family and do not transfer.
agent_relevance: A method can be a short priority list of conditional steps. For our agent, methods should be small and checkable.

source: Nau et al. (2003) SHOP2: An HTN Planning System (JAIR 20)
finding: SHOP2 won a distinguished performance award at the 2002 International Planning Competition (14 planners) and solved more problems than any other entrant.
numbers: 899 of 904 problems solved (99%). TLPlan 894. TALPlanner 610 (no numeric domains). Fully automated planners solved several hundred fewer.
limits: Hand-tailored track: the authors wrote the methods. SHOP2 was generally slower than TALPlanner and TLPlan; the three hand-tailored planners' speeds were polynomially related.
agent_relevance: With a good library, decomposition solves nearly everything. The cost moves to authoring the library, which is where an LLM could help and where it can err.

source: Nau et al. (2003) SHOP2: An HTN Planning System (JAIR 20)
finding: Hand-written domains are error-prone. At AIPS-2000 SHOP was disqualified from two domains because wrong methods produced incorrect plans. For SHOP2 the team wrote a translator from PDDL operators to avoid this.
numbers: Two domains disqualified in 2000. SHOP2 soundness holds only if the supplied methods and operators are correct.
limits: Single competition report.
agent_relevance: Methods are code that can be wrong. A decomposition must be checked against operator preconditions, never trusted as written (G2, G3).

source: Nau et al. (2003) SHOP2: An HTN Planning System (JAIR 20)
finding: SHOP2 states that HTN planning is Turing-complete and strictly more expressive than classical planning, and that translating classical to HTN is easier than the reverse. It adds interleaving of subtasks from different tasks and ordered method alternatives.
numbers: Features beyond SHOP: partial order of subtasks, ordered method alternatives, temporal operator translation.
limits: Interleaving subtasks gives up part of SHOP's simplicity of a known state at each step.
agent_relevance: Ordered method alternatives (try method 1, then method 2) map directly onto an operator choice list in O3.

source: Bercher, Alford, Holler (2019) A Survey on Hierarchical Planning (IJCAI-19)
finding: Survey of hierarchical formalisms. Plain HTN is undecidable (it can encode the intersection of two context-free languages). Adding task insertion (TIHTN) makes it decidable but loses expressivity; task sharing stays undecidable.
numbers: Cites Erol et al. 1996 for undecidability; every recursive TIHTN problem has a non-recursive TIHTN problem with the same solutions.
limits: Survey; names formalisms and systems but reports few runtimes.
agent_relevance: If decomposition may insert extra steps outside the method (task insertion), search gets easier but fewer procedures are covered. A design choice for O3: strict methods vs methods plus free repair steps.

source: Bercher, Alford, Holler (2019) A Survey on Hierarchical Planning (IJCAI-19)
finding: Reasons people use hierarchy: inject expert knowledge to speed search, give several abstraction levels for explaining plans to users, integrate users in planning, model plan libraries for plan recognition. Applications include Mars rovers, web service composition, narrative generation, personal assistants.
numbers: Goals are given as compound tasks, not as state descriptions; hierarchy acts like control rules.
limits: Motivation list, not measured against flat planning here.
agent_relevance: Hierarchy also serves explanation to the user, which fits showing a plan as steps with checks.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-Most Prompting (ICLR 2023)
finding: Ask the model to split a problem into easier subproblems, then solve them in order, each using earlier answers. On the SCAN length split this lifts a code model from chain of thought's 16.2% to 99.7%.
numbers: SCAN length split, code-davinci-002: standard 16.7%, CoT 16.2%, least-to-most 99.7%. text-davinci-002: 6.0 / 0.0 / 76.0. code-davinci-001: 0.4 / 0.0 / 60.7.
limits: Decomposition was shown by hand-written exemplars. SCAN is synthetic. The 99.7% also held on the other SCAN splits.
agent_relevance: Strongest evidence that explicit decomposition helps easy-to-hard generalisation. But the decomposition rules were given, not discovered.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-Most Prompting (ICLR 2023)
finding: Last-letter concatenation: the advantage grows with list length, and beats chain of thought even when chain of thought gets more examples.
numbers: L=12: least-to-most 74.0% (2 shots, 123 tokens), 8-shot CoT 38.4% (573 tokens), 4-shot independent-exemplar CoT 37.4%.
limits: Toy symbolic task; GPT-3 family.
agent_relevance: Decomposition is data-efficient on tasks that need length generalisation.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-Most Prompting (ICLR 2023)
finding: On GSM8K the overall gain is small but present on long problems. Almost every remaining failure could be solved with a manually written decomposition, so the model's own decomposition is the weak link.
numbers: GSM8K: CoT 60.97% to least-to-most 62.39% overall. Problems needing at least 5 steps: 39.07% to 45.23%.
limits: Small overall gain; no significance test reported in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Do not expect much from decomposition on tasks the model already solves. Gate O3 on difficulty (G1: only on a signal).

source: Khot et al. (2023) Decomposed Prompting (ICLR 2023)
finding: A decomposer prompt writes a program of sub-task calls to a shared library of handlers (prompted LLMs, trained models or symbolic functions). Handlers can be improved or swapped independently, and recursion handles long inputs.
numbers: Evaluated on k-th letter concatenation, list reversal, CommaQA-E and open-domain multi-hop QA (MuSiQue, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA) with GPT-3 and Flan-T5-XXL.
limits: Most headline numbers are in figures, not text. Decomposer prompts are hand-built per task.
agent_relevance: An LLM version of a method library. Handlers that are code (retrieval, string operations) match the 'code decides' principle.

source: Khot et al. (2023) Decomposed Prompting (ICLR 2023)
finding: A large arithmetic gain came from replacing a brittle answer-extraction pattern with a sub-task handler, not from splitting the maths. Credit for decomposition should be read with care.
numbers: MultiArith 78 to 95 (+17 pts) and GSM8K 36 to 50.6 (+14 pts) over CoT, from assigning answer extraction to a separate GPT-3 handler.
limits: The paper itself frames this as post-processing CoT for error correction.
agent_relevance: Part of what looks like decomposition benefit is parsing and format control, which code can do for free.

source: Khot et al. (2023) Decomposed Prompting (ICLR 2023)
finding: Recursive decomposition generalises to inputs longer than the examples. Splitting a list in halves and reversing the pieces keeps accuracy where CoT falls. A hard sub-task (find the k-th character) is broken into simpler steps when the model fails at it.
numbers: Figures 7 and 8: DECOMP outperforms CoT and least-to-most across input lengths N and across three prompt variants P1-P3 (exact values only in figures).
limits: Numbers read from figures only. Weaker models (curie) fall near zero for all methods.
agent_relevance: Recursive splitting of the same task on smaller input is a cheap O3 variant for list-like work.

source: Prasad et al. (2024) ADaPT: As-Needed Decomposition and Planning (NAACL Findings)
finding: Decompose only when the executor fails, recursively, with a depth cap. On ALFWorld with GPT-3.5 this beats ReAct, plan-and-execute, retry and Reflexion.
numbers: ALFWorld test, overall success: ReAct 43.3, Plan-and-Execute 43.3, Try Again 47.8, Reflexion 57.5, ADaPT 71.6 (dmax=3). Pick2 tasks: 11.8 for ReAct vs 52.9 ADaPT.
limits: GPT-3.5 completion model; baselines were given comparable numbers of LLM calls; Reflexion has a dedicated memory.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G1-style gating: decompose as needed, on a failure signal, not up front.

source: Prasad et al. (2024) ADaPT: As-Needed Decomposition and Planning (NAACL Findings)
finding: On WebShop and the new compositional TextCraft, as-needed decomposition beats static plan-and-execute. Static planning can even be worse than no planning.
numbers: WebShop: ReAct 32.0, Plan-and-Execute 17.0, Try Again 30.0, Reflexion 35.0, LATS 38.0, ADaPT 44.0 (dmax=3). TextCraft: ReAct 19.0, Plan-and-Execute 27.0, Try Again 15.0, Reflexion 32.0, ADaPT 52.0 (dmax=4).
limits: Test splits. Plan-and-execute lost 15 points against ReAct on WebShop but gained 8 on TextCraft, so the static-plan penalty is not universal.
agent_relevance: Fixed up-front decomposition can hurt. Decompose lazily.

source: Prasad et al. (2024) ADaPT: As-Needed Decomposition and Planning (NAACL Findings)
finding: Depth helps and is used in proportion to need. Going from dmax=1 to 2 gave the main gain; deeper recipes need deeper decomposition. Weak executors gain most.
numbers: TextCraft recipe depth 2: ReAct 26.9% to ADaPT 78.2% (mean depth used 1.9). Depth 3: 1.8% to 38.7% (mean depth 2.8). ALFWorld weak executor (atomic skills only): 3.3% to 41.7%.
limits: Gains are largest where the baseline is near zero. Same direction with GPT-4, LLaMA-2 70B and Lemur 70B, but open models score lower in absolute terms.
agent_relevance: The right decomposition depth depends on executor strength. O3 should deepen only when a leaf step fails its check.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Plan-and-Solve Prompting (ACL 2023)
finding: Ask for a plan first, then execution. Error analysis of 46 GSM8K failures under zero-shot CoT found missing-step errors in 12%, semantic misunderstanding in 27% and calculation errors in 7%; the plan prompt targets missing steps.
numbers: Zero-shot PS beats zero-shot CoT on all datasets (+2.5% average); PS+ is higher, e.g. Last Letters 75.2% vs 65.2%, and comparable to 8-shot CoT.
limits: GPT-3 only. The plan is free text from the same model with no check.
agent_relevance: A plan-first prompt reduces skipped steps but adds no outside check.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2023) PlanBench
finding: Direct (non-hierarchical) LLM planning on Blocksworld is poor. This is the baseline against which decomposition proposals are measured.
numbers: GPT-4 plan generation 206/600 (34.3%); Instruct-GPT3 41/600 (6.8%).
limits: Zero-shot or one-shot prompts; 600 Blocksworld instances.
agent_relevance: Models plan poorly alone, so hierarchy should come with external checks.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2023) On the Planning Abilities of LLMs: A Critical Investigation
finding: Autonomous plans from LLMs are rarely executable. Obfuscating the domain names collapses performance, which points to dependence on familiar names.
numbers: GPT-4 average success about 12% across domains. Blocksworld zero-shot 206/600 (34.3%). Mystery Blocksworld results sit in single digits to 14% across settings.
limits: NeurIPS 2023 models only.
agent_relevance: Naming of the domain, not structure, drove success. Method libraries that rely on familiar words may carry the same risk.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2024) LLMs Still Can't Plan; Can LRMs? (o1 on PlanBench)
finding: Reasoning models close much of the gap on small problems but degrade with size, and they fail on unsolvable instances.
numbers: o1-preview Blocksworld 587/600 (97.8%); Mystery Blocksworld 52.8%; Randomized Mystery 41.6%; 110 larger problems (6-20 blocks, 20-40 step plans): 23.63%. Unsolvable instances correctly flagged: 27% (Blocksworld), 16% (Randomized Mystery).
limits: Preliminary evaluation; far higher cost from hidden reasoning tokens.
agent_relevance: Long plans still break; a decomposition into sub-goals that code verifies is the usual remedy.

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024) Position: LLMs Can't Plan, But Can Help Planning in LLM-Modulo Frameworks
finding: Proposes the LLM as idea generator and external verifiers as critics in a loop. Cites back-prompting results in which a verifier lifts plan success.
numbers: Blocks World reaches 82% within 15 back-prompt rounds; Logistics 70%; obfuscated Mystery BW only about 10%.
limits: Position paper that reuses numbers from Valmeekam et al.; gain depends on a sound external verifier.
agent_relevance: Same design as our schema: model proposes, code checks. Gains shrink on obfuscated domains, so checks must be on structure.

source: Munoz-Avila, Aha, Rizzo (2025) ChatHTN
finding: A symbolic HTN planner that, when it has no method for a task, asks ChatGPT for a decomposition into primitive tasks and returns to symbolic planning. Verifier tasks make every returned plan sound: wrong LLM output is caught, not trusted.
numbers: Three domains: logistics, household robot, search and rescue. gpt-4-turbo, temperature 1, up to 5 attempts per test; about $30 per domain for tuning and all tests.
limits: Prototype on small, familiar domains. Non-deterministic even at temperature 0; some solvable cases failed on a first attempt. ChatGPT also returned task sequences for unsolvable problems, which the verifiers rejected.
agent_relevance: Closest published match to O3 plus code verification: the LLM fills holes in a method library, code checks the result. The authors propose to learn accepted decompositions as new methods.

source: Munoz-Avila, Aha, Rizzo (2025) ChatHTN
finding: Ablation by hiding one method or one compound task at a time: for most hidden items ChatHTN still solved the problem with 0 to 2 LLM calls. With the full domain it needs none. Hiding the top task equals pure LLM planning.
numbers: Table 2: e.g. hiding transportPackage method M2 took five runs, each with one call, to succeed; most other hidden items succeeded with 0 or 1 call per run.
limits: Table reports calls and success marks, not rates; few hand-built tests; no comparison to a flat LLM planner.
agent_relevance: Method libraries need not be complete if an LLM backstops the gaps. The count of LLM calls is a usable budget signal.

source: Gui et al. (2025) HyperTree Planning
finding: Top-down hypertree of subtasks built by an LLM from rule-like decomposition, expanded in stages (selection, expansion, pruning, decision), then a plan generated by self-guided planning. State of the art on TravelPlanner.
numbers: TravelPlanner validation (180 queries), Gemini-1.5-Pro: HTP success 36.1% vs best table baseline 8.9% (EvoAgent). GPT-4o: 20.0% vs CoT 4.4%. GPT-4o Blocksworld 54.7% vs CoT 35.5%; Mystery 8.7% vs 0.0%; Natural Plan Trip 36.9% vs 15.6%.
limits: With GPT-3.5-turbo HTP reaches only 1.7% on TravelPlanner and its commonsense pass rate (55.0 micro) is below CoT (61.0). Gains need a capable base model. Proprietary models.
agent_relevance: Hierarchical decomposition helps most when the base model is strong enough to write good sub-structure. Gate use by model capability.
